blocks.text: The Cold Fleet birds were at their morning feed when Joan Pettifer came into the Circuit Loft in her drainage boots, and their talk ran along the perches like rain along a gutter, soft and quarrelsome and never quite still. She did not take off her cap. She did not say good morning.
"You counted forty-one," she said. "Can you raise?"
I thought about it, because it was a true question and it deserved a true answer, and the only true answer I had was a small one.
"I don't know," I said.

Joan nodded as though I had given her a measurement. "Hobsmere have four days, no Wing and no money. Hamish is in the sanatorium with half the mere still in his chest. So you'll register this afternoon, won't you, and we'll find out at dusk?"

Behind me a Cold Fleet hen with a pale bar on her wing shouldered her neighbour off the trough and then settled beside him as if nothing had happened. I had fed that flight every morning for three winters. I knew which of them went to pieces in wind and which would come to my hand, and I knew that in all that time nobody had walked through the Loft door to ask for me.
"Yes," I said.

The conflict rule is short. A registered player may hold no place at the Circuit Loft and keep no private record of its flocks. The loft-master read it to me in the feed room, and then he shook my hand, which he had never done, and told me to hand the notebooks to the Court myself.

There were three of them, cloth-backed and swollen with fen damp, and I carried them up through Wenlode inside my coat, past the sluice running high and brown and a heron working the shallows below the weir, patient as a post. I walked slowly, and Joan let me.

The Ringing House stands at the top of the town, a long hall of grey stone that smells inside of ink and cold copper. A clerk of the Court sat at a desk under the high windows, a young man with ink on his cuff and a small iron die press at his elbow. He took my name and Joan's papers, and then he held out his hand for the notebooks.
I put them on the desk and kept my fingers on the top one a moment longer than I needed to.

In those pages was the Sedgeway cock who would only go into a crate backwards, and the Mallow birds that come in high and late on any evening with a west wind, and every Cold Fleet bird by its ring and its temper. There was the Eastfield hen with one white feather in her left wing, who always ate last and alone, and whom I had fed by hand all through my first winter. The clerk slid the notebooks into a Court envelope and sealed it. They would go back to the Loft that night, and some other hand would read them, or nobody would.
"I'm sorry to give them up," I said, because I was.
He looked up at me then, properly. "Yes, miss. People generally are."
He set a strip of copper in the die and pulled the lever, and the press came down with a sound like a latch: CCIII, and under it, 71.

"Seventy-one," he said. "Numbers go in order of registration. Every issue starts at two." He saw me waiting and went on, the way people do when they have explained a thing many times and still rather like it. "Number one is struck by standing order, Season Two, and kept here in the Ringing House. Unissued. The wording is, 'for the first Wing'."
"Which first Wing?" I said.
"That's the wording, miss."

He turned a page and read me the declaration rule in a level voice, as though reading out a tide table: sighted players may play, but must declare their sight at the Ringing, and an undeclared sighted player who is found out is suspended for one match. Then, without looking up, in exactly the same voice, he said that new Wings sometimes reported an extra shape above the flock; that it was the Loft's luck, an after-image of the sighted eye; and that naming it on a Reedbed was held to be bad luck and bad form.

He had not asked me anything, so I did not answer. I thought of Dorcas Ely writing forty with her head down. Joan, signing at the bottom of a long form, stopped with the pen lifted and did not look at me, and then went on signing.

While she paid, I went and stood under the charter. It hangs on the end wall in a black frame, brown ink on yellowed skin, in a hand that slopes the way reeds lean in a steady wind. One line near the bottom was written plainer than the rest, as if by someone else, and I read it twice.
The Long Final stands open until the first ring is opened.
Rings are closed and rings are cut. I had closed hundreds on young birds and never once opened one. I stood with my hands in my pockets and turned the word over, and could not make it lie flat.
"Train's at ten past two," Joan said behind me. "Come on."
Ezra Pollard met us at the far end of the Hobsmere causeway, on his own side, and did not come one step further.

The wind had gone round into the west while we were on the train, and the whole mere was moving under it in long dull ripples the colour of pewter. Out on the far reed a marsh harrier was quartering low with its wings held up in a shallow V, and every bird in the reed knew exactly where it was. I watched the harrier before I looked at the man. He was old and stooped, and when Joan said my name he looked at me a long moment and then up at the sky, as though the sky had asked first.
"Registered at noon," Joan said. "Wing for Hobsmere, if she can raise. You'll show her, won't you?"

Pollard said nothing. He turned and walked up the track, and we followed him. At the first gate he took a stub of chalk from his pocket and drew a short white mark on the post, and at the second gate he did it again, and at the third, and he did not look at the marks once he had made them.
"Can you tell if I can raise?" I asked him. "Before we start. Can you tell?"
He walked on. A little way past the third gate he said, "Frost tonight."
I waited.
"Birds come in tight on a frost," he said. "A tight roost..." He looked out over the reed where the harrier had been, and let the wind have the rest.
"A tight roost answers whatever's among it," I said. "So if I put anything over them, they'll tell me whether it's there."
He nodded once, slowly, and made a mark on the next gatepost.

The crew were waiting at the last gate, by Pollard's feed shed at the edge of the roost reed, with their bicycles laid down in the wet grass. Rhys Dorne was combing his hair in the shed window. Lucas Mbeki stood apart, with his back to the mere, and when I came near him he looked at the ground.
Joan had brought the club's ring box. Pollard turned a feed bin upside down for a table, and that was the Ringing.

I had closed rings on squabs at five days old, when the bird does not know anything has been done to it, but never on a person. A wrist is a different thing. Joan's was red with cold and rough with work, and I held it in my left hand to steady it and laid the copper round it with my right, CCIII 23, and pressed it closed with the pliers slowly, so as not to catch the skin. She watched my hands the whole time. Mercy's wrist was small and still. Abel's shook, very slightly. Rhys held his out with the cuff turned back and said, "Mind the shirt, Crate, it's new," and I minded it. Lucas gave me his without lifting his eyes. It was a clockmaker's wrist, narrow, with a fine burn scar across the back of the hand, and I closed his ring, CCIII 27, as gently as any of them. Then I closed my own, 71, and that was the hardest, because I had to do it one-handed and my hand was not steady.
"Ten's free," Pollard said. It was the most he had said at once. "No withy on her, so we stop short of ten. Nothing owed."
Then the roost came in.

They came from every quarter of the levels at once, small bands pouring along the dykes and joining into streams, and the streams into one body, thousands upon thousands of starlings, so many that the sound of them was a single long hush like surf on shingle. The light was going gold and then copper behind the far reed. The flock folded over itself and poured out thin as smoke and gathered again dark as a thrown net, and I stood among the crew with copper on my wrist and did not know what to do.
"Say it," Pollard said. "Same as you'd call a bird in."
I looked at Joan, and said her number. "Twenty-three."

Before anything moved above us, Lucas flinched. It was very small, a jerk of the head like a man who hears his name in a crowd, and it came a breath before anything had changed that anyone else could have seen. Then there was a bird-shape in the air above Joan, low over the reed, matching her as she shifted her feet, with a fleck of copper at its leg. Joan could not see it; she was watching me. Lucas was looking straight at it, and then he was looking at the ground again.
I kept that the way I keep a bird I cannot yet name: put by, on its own perch, to be looked at later.

I called the others one by one. Twenty-four, twenty-five, twenty-six, twenty-seven, seventy-one. Six shades flew over six heads, and within the minute there was a seventh at the far north-east edge of the roost, over no one, over the open reed, with old copper on its leg. I knew it at once and did not look at it long. Pollard had turned his back to that side of the sky.
"Each one watches seven," Pollard said. "Don't push the forty. Hold one."

I brought my ceiling down to the last bands coming in low, and asked the crew to close in under one small bird at the near edge of a stream. They ran together, Joan swearing at a rut, and my shades drew in around the bird, four and then five and then six. I watched its threads, the fine lines of its attention running out to its seven nearest, and saw six of them catch on my shades and swing. The bird turned. For three wingbeats, four, it went where I asked, and the stream did not come with it, and its fellows drew it back into the body of the flock as easily as a thread is drawn back through a needle's eye.
I tried again, and it went the same way. I tried a third time, and as it slipped from me I looked down at the wrists around me and counted copper, because counting is my work.
"Six," I said.
Pollard did not answer. The wind came across the reed and took whatever he might have said.
"Nine," he said, a little later, with his watch in his palm. "Drop them."

I called them down, and the roost poured on into the reed without them as if they had never been. The seventh shade stayed at the edge of the flock until the dark came down, and then I could not find it.

Pollard put his watch away and walked off up the track, past the chalked posts, before anyone could thank him. Joan went after him a few steps and called, "Ezra. Saturday. Will you stand by for the walk-down?"
He stopped at the gate. He did not turn round.
"No," he said, and went on.

Joan came back and cut our rings off with the wire snips from the ring box, and held my wrist a moment before she cut mine. "Don't ask him why," she said. "And don't ask me." That night I slept in the back bedroom of her cottage on the Hobsmere road and listened to the roost settling out in the dark, a long murmur going quieter until it was only the wind.

On Wednesday I went to see Hamish. The sanatorium stands on the one rise of ground for miles, among wind-bent pines, with rooks going in and out of their tops. Hamish Toller lay propped on pillows in a long ward, thinner than four days should make a man. His breath caught at the bottom of every breath.

I sat on the hard chair and told him I had registered. He knew; Joan had written. He did not say anything about the mere, and I did not ask, and the silence between us was not unkind. It was only full.
"Was it there?" he said at last. "Your training. Was it there?"
He did not say what. He did not need to.
"Yes," I said, because it had been.
Hamish looked at me a long while. Then he turned his face to the wall, and I sat and watched the rooks until the nurse came.
On Thursday evening Joan put it to the crew in the back room of the Dyke Arms, round a table ringed white by years of glasses.
"Sorrel needs a tether registered at Saturday's Ringing," she said. "Or she doesn't fly, and nor do we. One of you will take the withy, won't you?"
I looked at Joan, because Joan answers her own questions before she asks them, and this time she had not. She had her hands flat on the table and was looking at them.

Rhys leaned back in his chair. "Crate, I'd love to. But think it through. The tether stands behind the Wing for the whole walk-down, and the Levels Courier only ever gets the back of the tether's head. I have a profile. My left side was in the Courier twice last season. You don't put a profile like mine behind somebody."
Mercy laughed, a little. I did not, because I could see his hands.
"You went into the mere for Hamish," I said. "I saw you. I won't forget it."
Rhys stopped smiling. He looked at me for a moment, and then he reached over and straightened my collar, which did not need straightening, and said nothing at all.

Mercy said she was sorry, but she would be on the field, and she could not be near that water in the dark, not after Saturday. Abel had gone into the mere beside Rhys, and when Joan looked at him he wrapped both hands round his glass and they shook so that the beer moved.

Joan said nothing either. Outside the window the last light lay on Hobsmere Mere, the dull grey of a slate roof after rain, and a pair of mallard were going across it with their wakes spreading behind them until they touched the reeds on either side.
Somebody pushed back a chair.
"I'll take it," Lucas said. "The w-w... the withy. If you'll have me."
The only one who offered to take my withy was Lucas Mbeki, who had let Hamish walk into the mere five days before.
